title: Allow ABC mixins on states despite ABCMeta's _abc_impl bookkeeping
body:
Since #7136, a state that mixes in `abc.ABC` fails at class creation:

```python
class Mixin(ABC, rx.State, mixin=True):
    @abstractmethod
    def _value(self) -> int: ...
# StateValueError: State name `_abc_impl` is reserved by BaseState; use a different name instead.
```

`BaseStateMeta` is an `ABCMeta`, so `BaseState` has its own `_abc_impl`, and the reserved-name check then flags the `_abc_impl` it finds in `vars(ABC)` (and in any other `ABCMeta` mixin). `ABCMeta` writes `_abc_impl` onto every class it creates, so the copy an `ABC` mixin carries is bookkeeping, not a declaration. This change skips it only where it is inherited from a non-state base: declaring or `add_var`-ing `_abc_impl` on a state is still rejected. The tests cover `ABC` both as a plain mixin and under a state mixin, check that abstract methods are still enforced, and keep the reserved-name error for a state's own `_abc_impl`.

title: Fix double-close of listening socket on Windows
body: ### Type of change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ### Description On Windows, the development backend was closing its listening socket twice when releasing the port, which could close another socket that had reused the handle and cause it to fail with `OSError: [WinError 10038]`. The root cause is that both the socket object and Granian's `SocketHolder` wrap the same OS handle. On Windows, the `SocketHolder` closes the handle when dropped, so we must not also close it through the socket object. On other platforms, the `SocketHolder` never closes the handle, so we must close it through the socket object. The fix: - On Windows: call `detach()` on the socket object to release the handle without closing it, letting the `SocketHolder` close it when dropped - On other platforms: call `close()` as before, since the `SocketHolder` won't close it ### Changes 1. **`reflex/utils/exec.py`**: Updated `_close_shared_socket()` to conditionally call `detach()` on Windows or `close()` on other platforms 2. **`tests/units/utils/test_exec.py`**: - Simplified cleanup in existing tests to use the new `_close_shared_socket()` method - Added `test_run_granian_backend_closes_released_socket_once()` to verify the socket is closed exactly once and the handle isn't reused incorrectly ### Test Plan The new regression test `test_run_granian_backend_closes_released_socket_once()` verifies: - The socket is properly released and marked as closed - On Windows, the port remains bound (held by the `SocketHolder`) - On other platforms, the port is immediately bindable - A socket created after release can safely bind to port 0 without hitting a closed handle Existing tests pass with the simplified cleanup code. https://claude.ai/code/session_01NzRfCWGdwiJweGwficQitM

title: fix: emit every output line as JSON in reflex run --json
body:
Fixes #7196. Alternative to #7219.

## Problem

`reflex run --json` makes the logging pipeline emit JSON records, but anything written below the pipeline still reaches the terminal as plain text:

- `print()` in app code
- output from subprocesses and C extensions
- the `multiprocessing` traceback when a Granian worker fails to import the app (#7196)

#7219 fixes only the import-error case, through the private `granian._internal.load_target` API.

## Fix

In JSON mode, `reflex run` runs itself again below a small supervisor (`log.supervise_output()`):

1. The parent starts `python -m reflex <same args>` with `stdout` and `stderr` on pipes. An environment marker tells the child it is supervised, so it runs normally.
2. Every process the child starts (Granian workers, Node, subprocesses) inherits the pipes through normal `subprocess` inheritance. This works the same on Linux, macOS and Windows.
3. One reader thread per pipe converts output in batches of up to 64 KB:
   - a line that already is a JSON log record (an object with `level` and `message`) passes through unchanged, for example `JsonHandler` records from the child and its workers; this check runs first, so a record from another process never lands inside a traceback
   - a Python traceback becomes one `level: "error"` record with the full text in `exception`
   - any other line becomes a record with `logger: "stdout"` (level `info`) or `logger: "stderr"` (level `warning`)
4. The child runs with `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`, so `print()` output is not delayed by pipe buffering, and with `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` unless it is already set.
5. The parent forwards `SIGTERM` to the child, ignores its own Ctrl+C (the child gets the same interrupt), drains the pipes, and returns the child's exit code (`128 + signum` for a signal).
6. When a descendant outlives the child and still holds a pipe, the parent stops waiting after the reader has been idle for 0.5 s since the child exited.

## Cost

Measured with `reflex run --json --backend-only` on a blank app, median of 5 runs:

| | Time until `/ping` answers | Extra process |
|---|---|---|
| main | 0.73 s | — |
| this PR | 0.86 s | supervisor, 33 MB RSS |

The reader handles about 550k lines/s on a micro-benchmark, far above what an app logs.

## Verification

End to end with `reflex run --json --loglevel debug --backend-only`, an app that calls `print()` at import, and `raise RuntimeError("boom")` appended during the run: 0 lines that are not JSON records on stdout and stderr (main: 2 and 18). The traceback arrives as one record: `{"level": "error", "logger": "stderr", "message": "RuntimeError: boom", "exception": "Traceback (most recent call last):\n..."}`.

Also checked by hand: `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` to the process group in dev and prod `--backend-only`, and `SIGTERM` to the supervisor PID only. No hang, no leftover processes, all lines JSON.

Tests (all run on Windows too, except the `SIGTERM` one):
- `test_supervise_output_turns_every_line_into_json`: `print()`, `os.write(1, ...)`, `sys.stderr`, child processes, a child printing a JSON record and one printing other JSON, a JSON record inside a traceback, the logging pipeline, a crashing `spawn` worker, non-ASCII output, a final line with no newline, and exit code propagation.
- `test_supervise_output_drains_everything_for_a_slow_consumer`
- `test_supervise_output_does_not_wait_for_lingering_descendants`
- `test_supervise_output_forwards_sigterm`
- `test_output_pump_survives_a_gone_consumer`
- `test_run_supervises_output_only_in_json_mode`

## Known limits

- A plain line from another process that arrives inside a traceback ends the group early; each line is still valid JSON, but the grouping can mix.
- Exception group tracebacks and chained exceptions are not fully grouped; the remaining lines become separate records.
- Records made from plain lines carry no `pid` or `location`: the writer is unknown at the pipe.
- A prompt without a trailing newline stays in the reader until the next newline. `reflex run` has no prompts today.

title: fix(hosting-cli): keep app and deployment ids copyable in tables
body:
Fixes #7294. Alternative to #7349.

## Problem

`reflex cloud apps list`, `apps history` and `apps inspect` cut IDs short on a normal-width terminal. `apps inspect` puts all 20 fields in one row, so every cell shrinks to 2 characters. Users must use `--json | jq` to copy an ID.

title: fix(hosting-cli): report success from secrets update
body:

title: Fix buffered upload streams entangling events and dropping late deltas
body:
### Type of change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

### Changes To Core Features

- [x] Have you added an explanation of what your changes do and why you'd like us to include them?
- [x] Have you written new tests for your core changes, as applicable?
- [x] Have you successfully ran tests with your changes locally?

### Description

Two bugs in `EventProcessor.enqueue_stream_delta`, which buffered uploads (and custom routes) use to stream an event's deltas back over an HTTP response.

**1. The stream reused the root context's txid** (dccdc0574, 51e76b0e8)

The stream's context was `dataclasses.replace(self._root_context, ...)`, so its future and handler task were tracked under the root context's txid, which every top-level event names as its `parent_txid`. While a buffered upload was in flight (each of these reproduced before the fix):

- Every top-level event, from any client, was chained to the upload's future. Cancelling the upload (its client disconnecting) cancelled them too, and the upload's response stayed open until they finished.
- They inherited the upload's root generation, so a new navigation's `on_load` queued behind the previous page's unfinished one instead of superseding it.
- Concurrent uploads overwrote each other's `_futures`/`_tasks` entries: one stream ended early while its handler kept running untracked, and the other's future never resolved, hanging its response.

The stream's event now gets a context of its own: a fresh txid, no parent event, and the caller's OpenTelemetry context, so the handler span still nests under the upload request and records no `parent_txid`. The context is built in one step: CodSpeed flagged fork-then-`replace` at -4% on `test_yield_intermediate_update`, and a start/stream/stop round is back to `main`'s time locally.

**2. Deltas emitted after the stream ended were dropped** (587a4aefd)

Events chained from the streamed handler fork its context and inherit its delta emitter, so their deltas are streamed too, although the docstring said they were not. Streaming them is the behavior to keep: the frontend applies streamed chunks and socket messages through the same callbacks, and one channel keeps the chain's updates in order (browsers throttle XHR progress events, so a socket delta would overtake the handler's last streamed one). But anything emitted after the stream ended, such as by a recovery event the backend exception handler chains after the upload handler fails, went into a queue nobody read. The stream now takes deltas only until the chain finishes or the consumer leaves; later ones go out the usual way, and another token's delta is never yielded. The docstring now describes this.

**Also:** ports reflex-dev/reflex#7354's fix for the flaky `test_tree_phases_samples_a_real_tree` (627dfb11e), which failed `unit-tests (ubuntu-latest, 3.15)` here. The file matches that PR exactly, so whichever merges second applies it as a no-op.

**Not in this PR:** when the consumer leaves after the streamed handler itself finished, only the chained event being awaited gets cancelled; other running chained events continue.

### Test Plan

- Regression tests, each failing before its fix: `test_stream_delta_does_not_adopt_top_level_events`, `test_concurrent_stream_deltas_are_tracked_independently`, `test_stream_delta_emits_deltas_after_it_ends_normally`.
- Behavior pins: `test_stream_delta_yields_chained_event_deltas`, `test_stream_delta_sends_other_tokens_deltas_normally`, and `test_stream_delta_span_nests_under_caller` now asserts the span has no `parent_txid` attribute.

title: Stop top-level event spans naming the root context as their parent
body:
### Type of change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

### Changes To Core Features

- [x] Have you added an explanation of what your changes do and why you'd like us to include them?
- [x] Have you written new tests for your core changes, as applicable?
- [x] Have you successfully ran tests with your changes locally?

### Description

**Problem:** every top-level event is a fork of the event processor's root context, so its `parent_txid` was the root context's random txid. No future is ever registered under that txid, so event chaining was unaffected. But an event enqueued while a local span is current becomes an `INTERNAL` span, and `otel.event_span` recorded that meaningless txid as its `reflex.event.parent_txid`. Two ways this happens, both under the OpenTelemetry ASGI middleware's request span:
- the chunked upload endpoint (`_upload_chunk_file`);
- a custom API route calling `app.event_processor.enqueue`.

Websocket events escaped this only because they are `CONSUMER` spans. reflex-dev/reflex#7357 fixed `enqueue_stream_delta`; the general case remained.

**Solution:** fix it where the txid comes from rather than at call sites:
1. `EventProcessor.configure()` gives the root context an empty txid, since it belongs to no event.
2. `EventContext.fork()` sets `parent_txid=self.txid or None`, so forks of a context without a txid are top-level events.

`enqueue` already skips the parent-future lookup for a `None` parent. Top-level events still start their own root generation (supersession unchanged), and chained events still find their parent's future. `enqueue_stream_delta` already builds its stream context fresh (from reflex-dev/reflex#7357), so only its comment changed. That now matters for one more reason: a copy of the root would have no txid, and the events the stream's handler chains could not find the stream's future.

### Tests

- `test_top_level_event_under_local_span_names_no_parent_event`: enqueues a chaining event under a local `POST /api` span. The top-level span is `INTERNAL` under the request span with no `reflex.event.parent_txid`, the chained span still names the top-level event, and the future tree is unchanged. Fails before the fix: the attribute holds the root context's txid.
- `test_fork_without_txid_has_no_parent`: `fork()` of a context without a txid gives `parent_txid=None`, and a fork of that fork names it. Fails before the fix (`'' is not None`).
- `test_stream_delta_waits_for_chained_events`: the stream ends only once its handler's chained events are done.
  - It fails if the stream context loses its own txid.
  - `test_stream_delta_yields_chained_event_deltas` still passes in that case, because its chained event finishes before the stream closes.

Locally:
- `uv run pytest tests/units/reflex_base`: 561 passed.
- Full `tests/units`: 11030 passed, 81.24% coverage. This excludes `tests/units/reflex_bench/drivers/test_browser.py`, which fails the same way without this change because the container lacks the pinned Playwright browser build.
- ruff, pyright and the pre-commit hooks pass.

### Not changed

- `App.modify_state` forks the current context to rebind the token. An event enqueued inside `async with app.modify_state(...)` still names that fork's txid, which belongs to no event either. Changing that would alter chaining for handlers that call `app.modify_state`.
- Root contexts built directly (the `mock_root_event_context` fixture, the benchmark roots) keep a random txid, so their forks still name it. Harmless: nothing is registered under it.
- `EventContext.get().txid` outside any event is now `""` instead of a process-constant random id. Nothing in the repo reads it.

title: perf: cut per-event CPU on the runtime hot paths
body: Every backend event pays a fixed cost in the event processor and a per-value cost in the state machinery: reading fields and computed vars, wrapping values in mutable proxies, building the delta, encoding it to JSON and, with a redis or disk manager, pickling the touched states. Each of those paths did work per call that only has to happen once per class, per handler or per type, and a few did work that was never needed at all. Computed vars: a cache hit re-validated the whole cached value against the return type on every read (a 1000-element cached list cost ~1 ms per read; now ~0.2 us), the three cache attribute names were formatted per access, the last-updated timestamp was stored for every var although only interval vars read it, and marking a var dirty walked dependency dicts for names that have no dependents. The type mismatch is now logged once per computed value. Fields: scalar values skip the mutability check, and the dirty marking does not re-assign an already set touched flag through the dev-mode setattr hook. Mutable proxies: a proxy built for a list element no longer goes through the class lookup and the type-call dispatch, immutable values return before any tracking check in __getattr__, __getitem__ and __iter__, the dataclass frame check only runs for proxied dataclasses (via sys._getframe instead of a five-frame walk), and a method that is rebound to the proxy is no longer wrapped in a FunctionWrapper first. Event processor: the event context is built once per enqueue (fork takes the router_data), transaction ids come straight from os.urandom, the handler's coroutine-ness, background and supersedes flags and type hints are resolved once per handler, the per-event imports are hoisted, a handler that yields nothing skips the yield validation, the memory manager's modify_state and modify_state_with_links are plain async context managers instead of async generators, substate lookup resolves the class path once, and build_delta reads field values without constructing a proxy to unwrap. Serialization: json_dumps shares one encoder per set of separators instead of building a JSONEncoder per call, dataclasses serialize through a per-type serializer instead of dataclasses.fields() per instance, proxied values resolve their serializer once instead of dispatching twice, and StateUpdate serializes from a precomputed field tuple. State managers: redis persists every touched state of a tree in one pipeline instead of one write task (and one lock check) per state, deserializing a state updates the instance dict and drops the stale keys instead of filtering per key, the state-size check only runs on states over the limit, and the disk manager only derives a token for the states it writes. title: Fix oplock lease race with the lock updates subscriber
body:
### Type of change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

### Description

This applies the oplock fix proposed in https://github.com/reflex-dev/reflex/pull/6996#issuecomment-5923660175 as its own PR.

`test_oplock_contention_racers` failed now and then on CI, because one manager waited out the whole 5 s oplock hold time. The cause is a race in the oplock code itself:

- Only the keyspace notification for a contender's SADD on the waiters set can break a lease early.
- `_create_lease_break_task` took a lease as soon as SCARD returned 0. It didn't wait for the lock-updates subscriber to be listening.
- Redis pub/sub doesn't replay, so a winner that subscribed after the loser's SADD never got told to release.
- `_lock_updates_subscribed` was set as soon as PSUBSCRIBE was *sent*, not when Redis confirmed it, so waiting on it guaranteed nothing.

Changes in `reflex/istate/manager/redis.py`:
- `_subscribe_lock_updates` sets `_lock_updates_subscribed` when it gets the `psubscribe` confirmation from `listen()`.
- `_create_lease_break_task` only takes a lease once `_lock_updates_subscribed` is set. An event that arrives first does a single update without a lease and doesn't wait. That matters because a subscriber that never confirms would otherwise stall every event: a managed Redis that rejects `CONFIG` would add 2 s per event.
- `_ensure_lock_task_subscribed` returns early once subscribed.

Test changes:
- `mock_redis`'s `listen()` now delivers subscribe confirmations and no longer yields `None` for handler-dispatched messages, as redis-py does.
- `test_oplock_contention_racers` now awaits the broken lease before it checks `cancelled()`. Until its final flush finishes, the task doesn't report as cancelled.
- New regression test `test_oplock_lease_waits_for_lock_updates_subscriber`. It holds back the real `psubscribe` confirmation, then checks:
  - an event before the confirmation finishes promptly, with no lease and no lock left behind;
  - the next event after the confirmation takes a lease.

  It fails on `main`, if the flag is set on send, and if events wait for the subscriber.
- In `test_redis.py`, the fixture and the extra managers wait for their subscription before a test expects a lease. On real Redis the confirmation takes a round trip.

title: fix: don't log lifespan task cancellation at shutdown as an error
body:
## Problem

Each plain `async def` lifespan task gets this done callback:

```python
task_.add_done_callback(lambda t: t.result())
```

When the backend stops, Reflex cancels the task with `task.cancel(msg="lifespan_cleanup")`. Then `t.result()` raises `CancelledError` inside the callback. asyncio logs it at ERROR:

```
asyncio - ERROR - Exception in callback LifespanMixin._run_lifespan_tasks.<locals>.<lambda>() at reflex/app_mixins/lifespan.py:120
...
asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError: lifespan_cleanup
```

This happens once per coroutine task, per worker, on every shutdown and every dev hot reload. A normal shutdown looks like an app error. Tools that watch ERROR logs treat it as a failure (for example, the "App error detected" banner in Reflex Build).

#4075 reported the same traceback. #4083 fixed only the internal Windows hot-reload hack, so user tasks still hit it.

## Fix

At shutdown, cleanup cancels every running coroutine lifespan task, then waits for all of them, with a limit:

```python
for task in running_tasks:
    if task.done():
        continue  # already reported by its done callback
    task.remove_done_callback(_report_task_result)
    task.add_done_callback(_log_cleanup_error)
    task.cancel(msg="lifespan_cleanup")
if cancelled := [task for task in running_tasks if not task.done()]:
    _, pending = await asyncio.wait(cancelled, timeout=_LIFESPAN_TASK_CANCEL_TIMEOUT)  # 5 s
    # tasks still pending are logged by name
```

- `_report_task_result` calls `task.result()`, as the old lambda did. A task that raises, or cancels itself, while the backend is running is still reported by it.
- At cleanup it is swapped for `_log_cleanup_error`, which ignores the expected cancellation and logs any real error the task raises while handling it, as soon as that task finishes.
- All tasks are cancelled before shutdown waits, so their cancellation handlers run together, and a handler that waits on another task cannot deadlock.
- The wait is bounded at 5 seconds. A task that ignores cancellation is logged and shutdown continues to the token manager, state manager and health Redis cleanup. (Prod granian has no worker kill timeout, so without a bound a stuck task would hang shutdown.)

Verified on a real `reflex run` server (prod with 2 workers + SIGINT, and dev hot reload) with tasks that loop, raise, self-cancel, have slow cleanup, ignore cancellation, fail during cleanup, and wait on each other: no `lifespan_cleanup` ERRORs, real errors logged once, slow cleanup completes, no deadlock.

## Tests

- `test_lifespan_shutdown_cancellation_is_not_reported_as_error`: fails before the fix, passes after.
- `test_lifespan_coroutine_task_exception_is_reported`: a task that raises still reaches the loop exception handler.
- `test_lifespan_task_self_cancellation_is_reported`: a task cancelled before shutdown still reaches the loop exception handler.
- `test_lifespan_shutdown_waits_for_cancelled_tasks`: a cancelled task's cleanup has finished when shutdown returns.
- `test_lifespan_shutdown_cancels_all_tasks_before_waiting`: a cleanup that waits on a later task does not deadlock.
- `test_lifespan_shutdown_does_not_wait_forever_for_a_stuck_task`: a task that ignores cancellation is logged and shutdown continues after the timeout.
- `test_lifespan_task_cleanup_error_is_logged_and_shutdown_continues`: a cleanup error is logged and the rest of shutdown still runs.
- `test_lifespan_cleanup_error_is_logged_while_another_task_is_stuck`: a cleanup error is logged when that task ends, even while another task is still stopping.

I also checked it manually: a dev app with an `async def` lifespan task logged 1 error per hot reload before the fix and 0 after.

title: fix: type event handler calls with a fixed-arity overload per handler length, which ty can bind
body:
**This mitigates a ty bug, astral-sh/ty#4657.** ty does not bind a method whose `self` starts with a `TypeVarTuple` prefix (`self: "EventCallback[V, Unpack[Q]]"`) to its receiver. Every `EventCallback.__call__` overload has that shape, so under ty:

- calling a handler with its arguments, e.g. `on_click=State.remove(index)`, is reported as `invalid-argument-type`, plainly or with a `Var`
- no handler can be passed where a `Callable` of its arguments is expected

In a Reflex app checked with ty, that is most handler calls. pyright is not affected.

ty does bind a `self` without the prefix, e.g. `self: "EventCallback[V, V2]"`. This adds a fixed-arity overload for each handler length up to four arguments and each number of values passed:

```python
@overload
def __call__(self: "EventCallback[V]", value: V | Var[V]) -> "EventCallback[()]": ...
@overload
def __call__(self: "EventCallback[V, V2]", value: V | Var[V]) -> "EventCallback[V2]": ...
@overload
def __call__(self: "EventCallback[V, V2]", value: V | Var[V], value2: V2 | Var[V2]) -> "EventCallback[()]": ...
...
```

The `Unpack[Q]` overloads remain only for handlers of five or more arguments. That way each receiver still matches exactly one overload for a given number of values. Otherwise pyright would report a wrong value as `reportCallIssue` ("no overloads match") instead of `reportArgumentType`, and existing `# pyright: ignore[reportArgumentType]` comments at such calls, like the ones in `tests/units/components/core/test_upload.py`, would stop applying.

The types pyright infers do not change, and nothing changes at runtime. The extra overloads can be dropped once ty fixes the bug.

`tests/type_checking/event.py` covers full and partial calls, with plain values and `Var`s, plus handlers as callables:

- before: ty reports 12 errors (5 failed `assert_type`s with their 5 argument errors, and 2 `Callable` assignments), pyright none
- after: both are clean, and a full `pyright` run reports no errors

Handlers with five or more arguments still go through the `Unpack[Q]` overloads, so ty can still misreport some calls to them.
